Interpreting navigation sonar data for object detection: 
a feasibility study using the Ping360
Md Junayed Hasan1,2 · Somasundar Kannan2 · Ali Rohan2 · Amira Samy Talaat3
Received: 19 May 2025 / Accepted: 18 November 2025 
© The Author(s) 2025
Abstract
This study investigates the feasibility of repurposing the Blue Robotics Ping360—
a low-cost, mechanically scanned single-beam sonar—for underwater object detec-
tion beyond its navigation role. It addresses three key questions: (i) what challenges 
arise when interpreting navigation sonar data in cluttered or reflective environments; 
(ii) how effective is manual annotation when combined with segmentation models 
such as U-Net; and (iii) whether affordable sonar can support complex object-level 
perception. Controlled pool experiments were conducted to examine acoustic arti-
facts including reflections, shadows, and range-dependent distortions. A manually 
annotated dataset was used to evaluate classical and deep-learning-based segmenta-
tion methods. Results show that preprocessing—near-field exclusion, denoising, and 
polar resampling—significantly improves detection clarity. Leveraging GPU-accel-
erated and data-parallel processing, the framework achieves scalable, near-real-time 
performance aligned with high-performance computing principles. The dataset and 
code are publicly available to encourage further research in dynamic and multi-sen-
sor underwater perception.
Keywords  Underwater object detection · Robotic perception · Single-beam sonar · 
Ping360 sonar data · Affordable sensing technology · Underwater robotics

1  Introduction
In recent years, there has been a growing emphasis on exploring underwater 
environments for applications such as infrastructure inspection, maintenance, 
and object retrieval. Traditionally, these operations were carried out by human 
divers, often at significant physical and mental risk [1]. Advances in technology 
have since enabled the deployment of Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) and 
Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), which have revolutionized ocean 
exploration by automating complex tasks and reducing dependence on human 
operators [2]. Despite these technological advancements, underwater navigation 
and object detection remain challenging due to the limitations of optical sensors. 
Water turbidity, light attenuation, and scattering severely degrade visual data 
quality, making camera-based imaging unreliable in most sub-sea operations [3, 
4]. Although some short-range improvements in visual enhancement have been 
achieved through image restoration and color correction techniques, these solu-
tions are only effective in clear water and shallow conditions [5]. Consequently, 
alternative sensing technologies are needed to ensure reliable perception in turbid 
or low-light environments.
Sonar technology has emerged as a viable solution for underwater detection and 
navigation, as it operates using acoustic waves that can penetrate murky waters and 
function independently of ambient lighting conditions [6, 7]. Sonar systems are gen-
erally categorized into single-beam and multi-beam types. Multi-beam sonars pro-
vide extensive spatial coverage and high-resolution 3D reconstructions, but their 
cost and complexity limit accessibility for smaller research or commercial platforms 
[8]. In contrast, single-beam sonars—such as the Blue Robotics Ping360—employ 
a mechanically rotating transducer to sweep across a specified range, generating 2D 
polar representations of the surrounding environment. This scanning mechanism dif-
ferentiates it from fixed single-beam systems, which operate in a single direction 
without angular coverage. The Ping360, designed primarily for navigation and map-
ping, offers an affordable alternative capable of performing 360◦ scans at a center 
frequency of 750 kHz , with a 2◦ horizontal beamwidth, 30◦ vertical aperture, and a 
maximum range of 50 m [9]. Its open-source architecture and low-cost make it an 
attractive platform for academic and field research, though its potential for complex 
object detection tasks remains largely unexplored.
Recent progress in underwater imaging and structured-light techniques has 
improved scene reconstruction and obstacle detection in clear water environ-
ments [10–12]. For example, Han et al. applied deep CNNs for underwater image 
enhancement, while Ou  et  al.  developed structured-light frameworks for high-
precision mapping and collision-free navigation [11, 12]. However, optical and 
light-based systems remain highly sensitive to turbidity, illumination, and scatter-
ing—conditions in which acoustic sensing retains its robustness. Therefore, this 
study focuses solely on acoustic sensing to evaluate the feasibility of affordable 
sonar systems for underwater perception.
Existing research on sonar-based object detection has primarily concen-
trated on imaging sonar systems, which provide higher resolution but come at a

significant financial cost [13–15]. These studies often fail to address the inher-
ent differences between sonar and optical imagery. Single-beam systems like the 
Ping360 generate data with nonuniform resolution, strong speckle noise, acoustic 
shadowing, and reverberation, as noted by Karimanzira et al. [16]. While multi-
beam sonars can mitigate these effects through spatial averaging, single-beam 
sonars are more susceptible to noise and artifacts, which complicate object detec-
tion [17]. Nevertheless, their affordability—approximately one-fifth the cost of 
multi-beam systems—makes them appealing for low-cost or portable AUV opera-
tions. Prior studies suggest that advanced image-processing techniques and deep 
learning can enhance sonar-based detection [13, 15, 18], but these methods often 
rely on high-quality, high-resolution data rarely available in real-world single-
beam conditions.
McKay  et  al.  demonstrated that machine learning models fine-tuned for sonar 
data can improve detection accuracy even on simpler systems like the Ping360 [16]. 
However, such approaches often depend on idealized datasets that overlook practi-
cal challenges such as multipath reflections, surface interference, and object occlu-
sions. Moreover, many deep learning studies use synthetic or simulation-based data 
(e.g., Jiang et al.’s CycleGAN-based sonar-to-image conversion [19]), which may 
not accurately capture the variability and distortions inherent in real sonar measure-
ments. Forcing sonar data into purely image-based frameworks risks neglecting its 
unique acoustic characteristics—nonlinear propagation, intensity falloff, and geom-
etry-dependent reflections—which are critical for reliable detection in operational 
environments. Furthermore, manual annotation processes in existing studies are 
often under-described, leading to inconsistencies in ground truth quality and over-
estimation of model performance, as observed by Zhao et al. [19]. Factors such as 
object material, size, and positioning—which significantly influence detection reli-
ability—are rarely quantified in depth.
Although the focus of this work is underwater acoustic sensing, the compu-
tational framework—including deep learning–based sonar segmentation, GPU-
optimized model training, and data-intensive preprocessing—aligns with broader 
research areas in high-performance computing and AI-assisted signal processing. 
This interdisciplinary alignment supports efficient sonar data processing pipelines 
applicable to large-scale scientific and industrial deployments. From a computa-
tional standpoint, interpreting and segmenting sonar data in real time is inherently 
a high-performance computing (HPC) challenge. Each sonar scan generates thou-
sands of acoustic samples that must undergo denoising, resampling, and deep neural 
inference, all of which are computationally expensive and highly parallelizable. The 
data pipelines developed in this work employ GPU-based acceleration and multi-
threaded processing to achieve efficient throughput and reduced latency. This inte-
gration of deep learning, data-intensive signal processing, and HPC methods situ-
ates the present study within the broader domain of supercomputing research, where 
real-time and parallel performance are critical for operational deployment in autono-
mous underwater systems.
Our study specifically investigates whether the Ping360, originally designed for 
navigation, can be effectively repurposed for complex underwater object detection 
tasks. Rather than proposing new AI architectures, we use deep learning models as

To address these knowledge gaps, this work is guided by the following research 
questions. These are articulated below for clarity but can be read as extensions of 
our overarching objective to assess the computational feasibility of low-cost sonar.
1.1  Research questions
The primary research questions (RQ) addressed in this study are as follows:
•	 RQ1: What are the main challenges in interpreting navigation sonar data in clut-
tered or reflective environments?
•	 RQ2: How effective is manual annotation of sonar data in improving object 
detection when used with advanced segmentation AI models such as U-Net?
•	 RQ3: Can low-cost sonar devices like Ping360 typically used for navigation, be 
effectively repurposed for complex underwater object detection?
1.2  Contributions
In line with finding the answers to those questions, this research makes several key 
contributions:
•	 For the first time, we present a detailed investigation into the feasibility of using 
the Ping360 sonar device for object detection in underwater environments.
•	 We are releasing the raw collected data from the Ping360 sonar to enable future 
researchers to explore its potential usability, especially for those who may not 
have access to the device due to its cost, despite it being relatively affordable.
•	 We provide insights into the challenges of sonar data interpretation, including 
surface reflections, object shadows, and the importance of careful data annota-
tion for machine learning.
•	 We developed a segmentation dataset from manually annotated sonar images and 
demonstrated that the Ping360 sonar’s object detection performance is highly 
dependent on data preprocessing and careful interpretation, particularly when 
used with machine learning models like the U-Net segmentation algorithm.

2  Experimental setup details
This section describes the experimental setup used to evaluate the feasibility of the 
Ping360 sonar for underwater object detection. The focus is to explain the scanning 
mechanism of the sonar and the configuration of the test environment used for con-
trolled data collection.
The experiments were conducted in a small pool with dimensions of 6 m in 
length, 3 m in width, and 5 m in depth. The sonar was mounted 1.5 m from one side 
wall, placing it at the center of the pool’s width. Its transducer head was oriented 
along the pool’s longitudinal axis (x-axis) and aligned at 0◦ . The sonar performed 
a forward-facing scan covering a 180◦ sector (from −90◦ to +90◦ relative to the 
x-axis). According to the manufacturer specifications, the Ping360 operates with a 
horizontal beamwidth of 1◦–2◦ and a vertical aperture of 20◦–30◦ [9]. These narrow 
horizontal and wide vertical beams enable precise horizontal slicing of the environ-
ment, which is beneficial for isolating reflections from submerged objects at differ-
ent depths.
It should be noted that the Ping360 employs a mechanical scanning mechanism, 
where a full 360◦ sweep requires approximately 8 s . Although this delay did not 
affect results in our static setup, it may influence detection performance in dynamic 
environments or when deployed on moving platforms. This operational latency 
should be considered when integrating the Ping360 into real-time applications.
Two parallel wires were suspended across the pool length at different distances 
from the sonar to serve as anchor points for various objects, such as PVC pipes and 
an orange bucket. This configuration simulated small-scale floating or suspended 
offshore structures. The known positions of these wires provided ground truth ref-
erence ranges, allowing direct validation of sonar range estimates and detection 
accuracy. Specifically, Wire 1 was positioned 2 m from the sonar, and Wire 2 was 
positioned 4 m away, as illustrated in Figure 1. The setup facilitated systematic repo-
sitioning of objects between trials, enabling evaluation of how range and geometry 
affect sonar response.
The sonar scanned the environment incrementally, recording intensity values I 
within a range of 0–255 at each angular position. These intensity values represent 
the strength of acoustic reflections from objects within the field of view. The raw 
Ping360 sonar output is inherently represented in polar coordinates (range versus 
bearing). Each beam corresponds to a specific bearing angle, and each range bin 
encodes the reflected amplitude. For interpretability and machine learning analysis, 
these polar data are converted into Cartesian occupancy maps, where both axes rep-
resent spatial distance. Figure 2(b) shows the sonar data in its native polar form, 
whereas Figure  2(c) presents the same data projected into Cartesian coordinates, 
which are subsequently used in the processing pipeline.

3  Relevant technical details
The proposed framework for object detection using the Ping360 sonar consists of a 
sequential pipeline beginning with sonar signal acquisition, followed by signal fil-
tering and conversion into polar occupancy maps. The preprocessed data are then 
used to train a U-Net-based segmentation model for object extraction, and the per-
formance is compared with a traditional statistical thresholding approach. Figure 2 
partially illustrates the early stages of this workflow (data conversion), while sub-
sequent stages are discussed in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. In this section, we will discuss 
the details about the sonar propagation, the sonar data preprocessing methodology, 
and proposed architecture of U-Net algorithm.
3.1  Underwater sound propagation
In underwater environments, the propagation of sound behaves quite differently 
from its behavior in air. One of the key differences is the variability of the speed of 
sound, c (measured in m/s), which is not constant underwater [20, 21]. The speed of 
sound is influenced by several factors, including water temperature T (in ◦C), depth 
D (in meters), and salinity S (in practical salinity units, psu). This relationship is

In this study, as we are conducting experiments in freshwater environments, the 
salinity S is consistently set to 0 psu. Understanding and calculating the speed of 
sound underwater is essential because it directly impacts the performance and range 
of sonar systems. The system’s range is particularly dependent on the speed of 
sound, as well as additional parameters such as the sample period Sp (in seconds), 
sample distance Sd (in meters), and the total number of samples Sn . For this sonar 
device, the maximum scan range is not directly set by the user but is instead deter-
mined by these environmental and system parameters. The following equations

3.2  Sonar signal processing
Initial data filtering excluded unreliable points within 0.75 ms of the sonar head, as 
recommended by Blue Robotics [9], and beyond 6 ms, which corresponded to the 
full length of the pool and the maximum effective scanning range for the experimen-
tal setup. This filtering ensured that only valid data points within the useful scanning

mean intensity and 휎 is the standard deviation. This approach ensured the removal of 
noise while preserving significant reflections from objects in the pool environment.

Training and inference were executed on GPU-based hardware using TensorFlow’s 
data-parallel execution framework, which distributes the computational load across 
multiple cores. This implementation exemplifies the principles of high-performance 
computing, where parallelization of convolutional operations and asynchronous data 
loading drastically reduce training time. The computational optimization not only

4  Dataset details
The dataset (Table  3) consists of sonar data in its original format collected from 10 
experimental scenarios using the Ping360 sonar device. The purpose of these exper-
iments was to observe the Ping360’s capability to detect objects placed at varying 
distances from the sensor in a controlled pool environment. The data were captured 
using a consistent sonar configuration across all experiments, with the gain set to 
medium (G1) and 1200 samples collected per scan. In these experiments, objects 
were attached to two wires stretched across the width of the pool (which measures 
3 ms). Wire 1 was positioned 2 ms from the sensor and Wire 2 was positioned 4 ms 
away. The objects were hooked at various positions along the length of the wires, 
allowing for variable placements within the pool’s 3-meter width. This setup simu-
lates different object positions horizontally and vertically, offering a realistic repre-
sentation of object distribution in an underwater environment. The objects used in 
the experiments included two PVC pipes (one gray and one white) and two orange 
buckets. The first experiment was conducted with no objects present, serving as a 
baseline. Subsequent experiments introduced objects in different configurations and 
numbers, allowing for analysis of how object type, position, and density affect sonar 
detection. In Figures 3 and 4, the experimental setup and the collected occupancy 
polar map are presented for qualitative analysis in the subsequent section.

a Cartesian grid using Ping Viewer software, interpolating intensity values (0–255) 
over angular increments to form a spatial occupancy representation. The mirrored 
boundaries observed in Figure 5 arise primarily from multipath reflections, where 
acoustic waves reflect between opposing pool walls before returning to the trans-
ducer. In the occupancy polar map, the pool boundaries, including both height and 
width, are clearly displayed. The blue rectangular shape highlights the boundary 
bars visible in the occupancy map. The distance between the left and right pool 
width boundaries is 3 ms, which is also confirmed by the Ping Viewer software-gen-
erated occupancy map. The pool length boundary is at 6 ms, and this is also marked 
by a strong boundary, enclosed within a red box. Beyond this 6-meter mark, surface 
reflections begin to appear. A similar phenomenon can be observed after marking 
the pool width boundaries, where the light purple zone denotes the surface reflection 
area. In this setup, the sonar was positioned 1.5 ms from the side of the pool, placed 
precisely in the centrer of the pool’s width. The sonar sensor was oriented forward 
along the pool, with its transducer head aligned at 0 ◦ relative to the x-axis, and it 
was not submerged deeply in the water. Additionally, the pool is constructed with 
ceramic tiles, a reflective material that contributes to the surface reflections. When 
inspecting objects detected by sonar and their reported ranges, it is crucial to focus 
on the ROI, ensuring the most accurate readings. According to the data-sheet of the 
Ping360 sonar, the minimum working range is 0.75 ms [9]. Therefore, within the 
ROI, there is a significant amount of noise (indicated by darker colors) from 0.75 ms 
to 1 m. Moreover, some noise extends beyond this range, due to surface reflections. 
The pool is not entirely empty; it contains setup pipes and other objects that gener-
ate passive noise, further affecting the sonar readings. Therefore, when analyzing 
the data, special attention must be given to these factors to accurately interpret the 
results.

creating acoustic shadows, as highlighted in the orange annotation in Experiment 9

In Experiment 8, a bucket and a small white PVC pipe were placed in the same 
straight line, with the pipe in wire 1 and the bucket in wire 2. Based on the sonar

while the object at 4 ms (the bucket) should be partially obscured by the acous-
tic shadow of the first pipe, yet still somewhat detectable because the bucket 
is wider. This hypothesis was confirmed during the experiment, as the bucket, 
despite being behind the first object, was still detectable. Some reflections from 
the second object may have been observed, but they did not pose significant dif-

without being hidden under an acoustic shadow. The absence of overlapping

in this case, a bucket, was placed in front of PVC pipes. The detection of the bucket

shadow behind it. However, because of the bucket’s dimensions, the shadow was not as

onstrates the correlation between an object’s size and the extent of the acoustic shadow

In Experiments 4 and 5, no issues were encountered with acoustic shadows or surface 
reflections, allowing for clear detection of objects at both distances. The sonar was able 
to capture the objects without interference, as no objects were positioned in a way that 
would block sound waves and create shadowed areas. The absence of significant reflec-
tions from the pool’s surface or nearby objects further contributed to the clean detec-
tion in these experiments.
5.2.8  Observation summary
Through these experiments, the impact of acoustic shadows in sonar imagery is 
clearly demonstrated. The presence of an object directly blocks sonar waves, prevent-
ing them from reaching areas behind the object and creating shadowed regions where 
no returns are detected. The size, shape, and alignment of objects are critical factors 
in determining the extent and intensity of these shadows. Additionally, surface reflec-
tions from the pool can contribute to or amplify acoustic shadow effects, particularly in 
complex setups involving multiple objects. This understanding is crucial for accurate 
sonar data interpretation and for mitigating the effects of acoustic shadows in practical 
applications.

5.3  Challenges in sonar data annotation: addressing ambiguities 
and operational factors
When defining objects in sonar imagery, as shown in the occupancy maps in Fig-
ures  3,   4, and particularly in Figure  6, where the ROI-based polar occupancy 
map highlights objects with bounding boxes, several challenges emerge. Take, for 
instance, Experiment 8 in Figure 6; can we confidently state that the bounding boxes 
represent a PVC pipe and a bucket? Not necessarily. While we can infer the presence 
of potential obstacles, accurately distinguishing between different object types is dif-
ficult without additional context. This highlights one of the key challenges in sonar-
based object detection: interpreting ambiguous or unclear sonar data. To address 
this challenge, each sonar image was independently annotated by two expert anno-
tators with prior experience in AUV/ROV operations. Annotation consistency was 
assessed using the Cohen’s Kappa coefficient ( 휅= 0.87 ), indicating strong agree-
ment. Discrepancies were resolved via joint discussion. The annotation guideline 
required labeling only high-confidence object reflections within the ROI, excluding 
ambiguous low-intensity zones or noise reflections.
5.3.1  Challenges in object annotation
In scenarios like this, when annotating data for models such as U-Net-based object 
detection, it becomes essential to incorporate pre-knowledge or human supervi-
sion. The visible sonar image alone may not provide enough information to con-
fidently label an object. Thus, experts, such as ROV/AUV pilots who have years 
of experience navigating underwater environments, play a critical role. They bring 
domain knowledge that helps guide the annotation process, suggesting what specific 
features might represent. This expert input, combined with the sonar data, enables 
more accurate bounding box placements and labeling, reducing the margin for error 
that typically arises when interpreting sonar imagery. For instance, in the provided 
image, the two bounding boxes indicate areas of interest. However, without external 
knowledge, it is difficult to discern whether the objects are PVC pipes, buckets, or 
other obstructions. Here, a domain expert would likely know that specific patterns 
or shapes in the data correspond to certain object types, which would be invaluable 
during the annotation process.
5.3.2  Impact of sensor position and orientation
Another critical factor is the position and orientation of the sonar sensor. In this 
case, the sonar sensor is positioned at 0 ◦ horizontal, with its transducer head aligned 
along the x-axis. While this setup provides one view of the underwater environment, 
it limits what can be seen. If the sensor were angled differently—such as being tilted 
downward like a torchlight beam—it might reveal more distinct shapes or features 
of objects. However, the visibility of such shapes would still depend heavily on the 
operating conditions, such as water clarity, object material, and the acoustic proper-
ties of the environment. For instance, a downward-facing sensor might reveal more 
detail about the height or vertical structures of objects in the water, which would be

tion can drastically affect the quality of the sonar image and, consequently, the accu-

5.3.3  Gaps in existing research
In the introduction, we referenced various studies that apply image-processing tech-
niques and AI models to sonar data for object detection [15, 18, 24–30]. While these 
models often report high accuracy in controlled test datasets, they tend to overlook 
real-world complexities such as the acoustic shadow effects, cluttered environments, 
or reflective surfaces. These studies primarily focus on pixel-level precision in sonar 
imagery, yet rarely discuss the deeper challenges of sonar data interpretation and 
annotation. The annotation process in these studies is often assumed, but critical 
details such as whether subject matter experts contributed to the process, the mount-
ing angle of the sonar, or how the ROV/AUV’s movement and positioning altered 
the sonar angle and subsequently affected the collected data are frequently left unex-
plained. Without accounting for these factors, the reported high accuracy of these 
models can be misleading when applied to more complex or real-world environ-
ments, where ambiguity in sonar data is common.
Therefore, in the next section, we will proceed with annotating the data based on 
the observations we have made. Specifically, we will create segmentation masks for 
the detected objects, categorizing each mask as an object class. Using these anno-
tations, we will evaluate the performance of the U-Net model. According to our 
hypothesis, by applying the data processing techniques discussed earlier—such as 
noise reduction—we anticipate an improvement in accuracy. Additionally, increas-
ing the training duration or initializing the model with well-tuned weights could fur-
ther enhance the results. While more complex models, as discussed in the literature, 
might yield even higher accuracy.
6  Result analysis of segmentation model
This study utilizes the U-Net segmentation model to explore the Ping360 sonar’s 
potential for object detection. U-Net was chosen for its proven capability in han-
dling segmentation tasks with limited training data, a common scenario in sonar-
based applications. Its architecture, featuring an encoder–decoder structure with 
skip connections, allows for precise localization and efficient learning of spatial fea-
tures from sonar images. These qualities make U-Net particularly suitable for tasks 
where high-resolution output is essential, such as detecting underwater obstacles in 
noisy or low-quality acoustic data. While the primary focus of this manuscript is to 
demonstrate the feasibility of applying deep learning for sonar-based object detec-
tion rather than evaluating the performance of multiple models, U-Net serves as a 
strong baseline due to its widespread adoption and effectiveness in similar appli-
cations. Therefore, to evaluate the performance of our U-Net-based object detec-
tion model, we collected approximately 700 samples across various experimental 
scenarios. Each sample was manually annotated, creating segmentation masks by

(F1S), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Boundary IoU (BIoU), and BIoU/Boundary F1

We performed two MExps to evaluate the U-Net model’s segmentation per-
formance. In MExp1, we used the polar occupancy map with data preprocessing, 
including noise reduction techniques. In MExp2, we used the raw polar occu-

hypothesis was that the preprocessed dataset would yield better performance due

the model trained on raw data reached an accuracy of 88%. This demonstrates the 
importance of preprocessing in improving segmentation accuracy.
Table 4 shows that MExp 1, which involved preprocessing the data, outperformed

preprocessing allowed the model to focus more effectively on the true object bound-

model’s ability to handle sonar data and leads to higher segmentation performance, 
making it critical for achieving accurate object detection in complex environments.

7  Response to our research questions
This study examined key challenges in interpreting and processing sonar data for 
underwater object detection using the low-cost Blue Robotics Ping360 sonar. The 
results are discussed here in relation to the three research questions (RQs) that 
guided this work.
7.1  RQ1: challenges in interpreting navigation sonar data
The first research question addressed the difficulties of interpreting navigation sonar 
data in cluttered or reflective environments. Across all experiments, we observed 
characteristic artifacts such as acoustic shadows, surface reflections, and near-field 
noise—particularly when multiple objects were present or when the pool’s ceramic 
boundaries produced strong reflections. For instance, in Experiment 8, overlapping 
acoustic shadows caused by closely spaced objects masked targets located behind 
them, complicating detection. Similarly, surface reflections generated spurious high-
intensity returns beyond the pool’s physical boundaries, distorting the polar occu-
pancy maps. These observations emphasize that sonar-based object detection is 
inherently affected by environmental geometry and material composition, requiring 
careful interpretation that goes beyond standard image-analysis assumptions. Unlike 
optical imagery, sonar data encodes acoustic amplitude modulated by geometry, 
orientation, and reflectivity, which necessitates domain-specific preprocessing and 
context-aware interpretation.
7.2  RQ2: effectiveness of manual annotation with advanced AI models
The second research question evaluated whether manual annotation can improve 
object detection when combined with learning-based segmentation models such 
as U-Net. Our results confirm that expert-guided annotation substantially enhances 
model accuracy by providing physically consistent labels that capture acoustic dis-
tortions and shadowing effects. However, the study also revealed that sonar data 
cannot be treated as a conventional computer vision problem. The acoustic nature 
of sonar images introduces ambiguities—e.g., intensity gradients caused by beam 
spreading or object tilt—that cannot be resolved through automated segmentation 
alone. In Experiment 8, for example, the sonar data distinctly captured the PVC pipe 
and bucket, yet differentiating between these objects required human contextual 
interpretation. Therefore, while models like U-Net can learn general object bound-
aries, their effectiveness depends heavily on preprocessing quality and domain-
informed labeling. Manual annotation remains essential, not as a substitute for auto-
mation but as a calibration tool that grounds AI training in physical reality.
7.3  RQ3: feasibility of repurposing low‑cost sonar for object detection
The third research question examined whether low-cost navigation sonars like the 
Ping360 can be repurposed for object detection. The findings indicate that the device

performs reliably for isolated and moderately sized targets within close range, typi-
cally up to 4 m . However, in scenes with overlapping or reflective objects, detection 
reliability decreases sharply due to the limited angular resolution ( 1◦–2◦ ) and sen-
sitivity to beam interference. Smaller or more distant targets ( < 1 m apparent size) 
were often indistinguishable from background clutter. These limitations suggest that 
while the Ping360 can support basic object detection in structured, static environ-
ments, achieving robust segmentation in complex settings requires advanced pre-
processing, noise suppression, and expert-guided annotation.
Although this study used a static environment, real-world implementation on 
AUVs or ROVs introduces additional challenges, including platform motion, scan 
latency, and real-time processing constraints. The Ping360’s mechanical rota-
tion ( ∼8 s per 360◦ ) limits temporal resolution, necessitating motion compensation 
and multi-sensor fusion for dynamic deployments. Factors such as vehicle motion, 
sonar latency, and variable salinity gradients can alter acoustic propagation. Adap-
tive scanning strategies—e.g., sector-focused scanning combined with IMU-based 
compensation—could mitigate temporal delays. On-board inference using compact 
architectures such as MobileNetV3-Seg [33] or YOLOv8-Seg [34] (optimized via 
TensorRT) may enable near-real-time segmentation at 8–10 fps on edge GPUs like 
NVIDIA Jetson Orin. Future studies should therefore evaluate such integrated sys-
tems under varying environmental conditions (temperature, salinity, turbidity) to 
enhance operational robustness. Overall, our results highlight the need for expert-
guided annotation, advanced preprocessing, and task-specific model adaptation to 
fully leverage affordable sonar devices for complex underwater perception.
8  Conclusions
This study presents the first comprehensive experimental evaluation of the Blue 
Robotics Ping360 sonar for complex underwater object detection, assessing the fea-
sibility of repurposing this affordable, open-source sensor beyond its conventional 
navigational role. Motivated by the need for cost-effective alternatives to high-end 
imaging sonars, a controlled set of experiments characterized the Ping360’s detec-
tion performance across different object configurations and environmental condi-
tions. The results confirm that the device can accurately detect isolated objects in 
static environments but struggles to discriminate between multiple or closely spaced 
targets due to its coarse angular resolution and susceptibility to surface reflections 
and noise. Without appropriate preprocessing and expert supervision, the raw sonar 
data lacks sufficient clarity for robust segmentation.
Despite these constraints, the study contributes three major outcomes. First, it 
establishes a publicly available, manually annotated sonar dataset that serves as 
a benchmark for AI-driven underwater perception. Second, it demonstrates that 
domain-informed preprocessing and labeling significantly improve segmenta-
tion reliability, underscoring the importance of expert knowledge in training data 
preparation. Third, it identifies key limitations of low-cost mechanical sonars, 
providing actionable guidance for future system design and deployment. In addi-
tion to its experimental contributions, this study demonstrates the computational

significance of employing HPC techniques for sonar data interpretation. By 
exploiting GPU parallelism and efficient data pipelines, the framework achieves 
high-throughput processing suitable for scalable deployment in real-time autono-
mous systems. These results reinforce the role of supercomputing as an enabling 
technology for underwater perception, bridging acoustic sensing with modern AI-
driven, high-performance signal analysis.
Future work should extend these findings to dynamic scenarios involving mov-
ing AUVs/ROVs and variable environmental parameters such as salinity, tem-
perature, and turbidity. Research into semi-supervised and self-supervised learn-
ing frameworks may help reduce reliance on extensive manual annotation, while 
multi-sensor fusion—combining sonar with optical or LiDAR sensing—could 
enhance spatial resolution and environmental awareness. Furthermore, integrat-
ing adaptive scanning and real-time inference pipelines could transform afford-
able sonars like the Ping360 into practical tools for mobile robotics and envi-
ronmental monitoring. Overall, this study lays the groundwork for advancing 
low-cost sonar-based perception, demonstrating that with proper processing and 
domain expertise, accessible acoustic sensors can play a significant role in the 
democratization of underwater robotics research.

Abstract: This study investigates the feasibility of repurposing the Blue Robotics Ping360— a low-cost, mechanically scanned single-beam sonar—for underwater object detec- tion beyond its navigation role. It addresses three key questions: (i) what challenges arise when interpreting navigation sonar data in cluttered or reflective environments; (ii) how effective is manual annotation when combined with segmentation models such as U-Net; and (iii) whether affordable sonar can support complex object-level perception. Controlled pool experiments were conducted to examine acoustic arti- facts including reflections, shadows, and range-dependent distortions. A manually annotated dataset was used to evaluate classical and deep-learning-based segmenta- tion methods. Results show that preprocessing—near-field exclusion, denoising, and polar resampling—significantly improves detection clarity. Leveraging GPU-accel- erated and data-parallel processing, the framework achieves scalable, near-real-time performance aligned with high-performance computing principles. The dataset and code are publicly available to encourage further research in dynamic and multi-sen- sor underwater perception.
